sections.heading: A bucket stays in one Region and names each object by a unique key

plan.problem: An application must keep millions of recordings and read each one back by name. It needs no disk and no folder tree.
trace: **Create the bucket.** [a bucket is a container for objects] (s3-object-storage-definition), created in [the AWS Region where the bucket will reside] (s3-bucket-region-fixed); you [can't change its name or Region] later (s3-bucket-name-region-fixed). By default the name is [unique across all AWS accounts] in the partition (s3-bucket-name-global-namespace-default).

**Put an object.** An object is [a file and any metadata] (s3-object-storage-definition), stored under a key, the [unique identifier for the object within the bucket] (s3-object-key-unique-in-bucket). A key such as customer-17/2026/call.wav looks like a path, but the bucket has a [flat structure] and folders come only from [key name prefixes and delimiters] (s3-flat-namespace-no-folders).

**Store it.** The multi-zone classes keep the object across [a minimum of three Availability Zones] (s3-durability-three-az-design), and S3 runs [end-to-end integrity checking] on the upload (s3-faq-durability-integrity-checks).

**Read it back.** A read after a successful write [immediately receives the latest version] (s3-faq-consistency-read-latest); an overwrite is atomic, so a reader gets old or new data, [never partial or corrupt data] (s3-single-key-updates-atomic).
plan.table: Object, block or file storage (columns: Storage | Reached through | Fits): object storage (Amazon S3) | [an application programming interface (API) over the internet] (s3-object-storage-api-read-heavy) | [read-heavy workloads]; block storage | [direct-attached to a compute instance] (s3-vs-block-storage-direct-attached) | [fast and consistent I/O operations]; file storage | [industry-standard protocols like NFS and SMB] (s3-vs-file-storage-shared-mount) | [shared data across multiple compute instances]. Chapters 22 and 23 own EBS and EFS: an xref, no detail.
plan.why: Why one Region? You decide where the data lives: objects [never leave the Region unless you explicitly transfer] them (s3-objects-stay-in-region), which matters for personal data such as call recordings.
plan.exam_signal: "store any amount of data and serve it to applications over HTTP" points to Amazon S3, because the total volume and the number of objects are [unlimited] (s3-faq-storage-unlimited); "a shared file system that many instances mount" points to file storage (chapter 23).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: four bucket types and a new namespace. S3 has [four types of buckets] (s3-table-and-vector-buckets). A general purpose bucket holds [all storage classes except S3 Express One Zone] (s3-faq-general-purpose-bucket-classes, or s3-general-purpose-bucket-all-classes); a directory bucket lives in [a single AWS Availability Zone] for [single-digit millisecond PUT and GET latencies] (s3-directory-bucket-single-az-express). Since [2026-03-12] you can create buckets in an [account regional namespace] instead of the global one (s3-change-account-regional-namespace-2026-03). S3 Files gives file system access while [Your authoritative data always remains in S3] (s3-files-built-on-efs-data-stays-in-s3). At most 110 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: S3 stores objects by key, in a bucket that stays in one Region. The thing to watch is that a folder is only part of the key name.
plan.stop_and_answer: Worker A overwrites transcript.json. A second later, worker B reads the same key. Can worker B get a mix of the old and the new file? Answer: no; updates to one key are atomic, so B gets old or new data, [never partial or corrupt data] (s3-single-key-updates-atomic), and a read after the successful write [immediately receives the latest version] (s3-faq-consistency-read-latest).

sections.heading: A single PUT stops at 5 GB so large uploads use multipart upload

plan.problem: A customer uploads a four-hour recording over a weak office connection. If one request carries the whole file, a failure near the end means starting again.
trace: **One request.** A single PUT uploads an object of at most [5 GB] (s3-single-put-max).

**Start a multipart upload.** S3 returns an upload ID that every later part request must carry: [this upload ID is required] (s3-multipart-anonymous-cannot-initiate). Each part is [5 MiB to 5 GiB] (s3-mpu-part-size), up to [10,000 parts] (s3-mpu-max-parts); you can [upload parts in parallel to improve throughput] and [retransmit that part without affecting other parts] (s3-multipart-upload-parallel-parts-throughput).
**Complete it.** S3 assembles the object from its parts; one object can be up to [50 TB] (s3-object-max-size). AWS calls multipart a best practice from [100 MB] (s3-mpu-recommended-threshold).

**Or leave it open.** An upload has [no expiry] (s3-mpu-no-expiry), and the stored parts are billed until you [must either complete or stop the multipart upload] (s3-multipart-upload-incomplete-parts-billed). A lifecycle rule with [AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload] removes them (s3-lifecycle-abort-incomplete-multipart); S3 Storage Lens finds buckets without that rule (s3-storage-lens-find-buckets-without-abort-mpu-rule).

**Upload from far away.** With Transfer Acceleration the client sends to [s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com] (s3-transfer-acceleration-endpoint-and-naming), enters at a CloudFront edge location and travels [over an optimized network path] (s3-transfer-acceleration-how-it-works); when it is not likely to be faster, [we will not charge for that use] (s3-transfer-acceleration-no-charge-when-not-faster).
plan.table: Which upload or read tool (columns: Need | Use | Watch): one object up to the single PUT limit | single PUT | [5 GB] (s3-single-put-max); larger objects or a weak link | multipart upload | parts billed until completed or stopped; clients on other continents | Transfer Acceleration | bucket name [must not contain periods] (s3-transfer-acceleration-endpoint-and-naming); a faster download of one large object | byte-range fetches, which [fetch different byte ranges] (s3-byte-range-fetch-parallel) | one request per range; many requests each second | spread keys over prefixes: [3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE] and [5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second] per prefix (s3-prefix-request-rate-baseline) | [503 (Slow Down) errors] while S3 scales (s3-request-scaling-gradual-503).
plan.why: Why parts? A failed part is sent again on its own, so a broken connection costs one part, not the whole recording: S3 lets you [retransmit that part without affecting other parts] (s3-multipart-upload-parts-parallel).
plan.exam_signal: "large uploads fail and must restart from the beginning" points to multipart upload; "users around the world upload to one bucket" points to S3 Transfer Acceleration (s3-transfer-acceleration-when-to-use).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: event notifications after an upload. When an object arrives, S3 can send an event to [Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS] or [directly to AWS Lambda] (s3-faq-events-destinations); an SNS, SQS or Lambda destination must be in the [same AWS Region as your Amazon S3 bucket] (s3-event-destinations-same-region). Events are [delivered at least once] (s3-event-notifications-at-least-once-seconds) and [aren't guaranteed to arrive in the same order] (s3-event-notifications-no-order-duplicates). An SQS FIFO queue is not a direct destination; [you can use Amazon EventBridge] (s3-event-notifications-no-fifo-destinations). A function that writes back to the same bucket [could cause an execution loop] (s3-event-notification-recursive-loop). Chapter 31 owns event-driven designs. At most 110 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: for big files, upload in parts that travel in parallel. The thing to watch is unfinished uploads, which still cost money.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team uploads 2 GB video files with one PUT each, from an office on another continent. Uploads often fail near the end. Is the single PUT size limit the cause, and what helps? Answer: no, the files are below the single PUT limit (s3-single-put-max); multipart upload lets a failed part be resent alone (s3-multipart-upload-parts-parallel), and Transfer Acceleration shortens the long path (s3-transfer-acceleration-how-it-works). Do not repeat the 2 GB value in the reveal without a link; say 'the files are below the limit'.

sections.heading: S3 allows a request only when a policy allows it and nothing denies it

plan.problem: A role in an analytics account must read recordings in the production account's bucket. Several policies apply to that one request, and one of them may say no.
trace: **Start from no.** Buckets and objects [can be accessed only if you explicitly grant] access (s3-private-by-default).

**Collect the policies.** S3 [evaluates all the relevant access policies] (s3-authorization-evaluation-order): the caller's identity-based policy and the bucket policy, a [resource-based AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy] that only the bucket owner can attach: [Only the bucket owner can associate a policy] (s3-bucket-policy-owner-only).

**Look for a deny.** [If there is an explicit deny set], S3 refuses the request (s3-authorization-evaluation-order); for example, a Deny with [aws:PrincipalOrgID] stops every caller outside the organization (s3-bucket-policy-deny-outside-org).

**Count the allows.** In one account, [either a bucket policy or a user policy] is enough (s3-same-account-bucket-or-user-policy). Across accounts the caller needs [permission from both the parent AWS account] and the bucket owner (s3-authorization-both-accounts-must-allow).
plan.table: Who must allow (columns: Caller | Identity-based policy | Bucket policy | Result): same account | allows | silent | allowed; same account | silent | allows | allowed; other account | allows | silent | denied; other account | allows | allows | allowed; any account | allows | has a matching Deny | denied. One term per result: allowed, denied (use 'implicit deny' only if the IAM chapter's wording is linked).
plan.why: Why two allows across accounts? Each account controls its own side: the caller's account decides what its role may do, and the bucket owner decides who may touch the bucket (s3-authorization-both-accounts-must-allow).
plan.exam_signal: "grant another AWS account read access to the bucket" points to a bucket policy that names the other account's role, plus an identity-based policy in that account; not an object ACL, because AWS recommends to [keep ACLs disabled] (s3-acls-not-recommended).
plan.body_extras: One or two sentences: Object Ownership defaults to [Bucket owner enforced] and [all ACLs are disabled] (s3-object-ownership-default-bucket-owner-enforced); a request that sets another ACL fails with [AccessControlListNotSupported] (s3-acl-writes-fail-when-bucket-owner-enforced).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: older ACL buckets, delegation and organization limits. With Object Ownership set to Object writer, [that account (the object writer) owns the object] (s3-object-writer-owns-object-when-acls-enabled), and bucket policy permissions [don't apply to objects that are owned] by other accounts (s3-bucket-policy-not-other-accounts-objects). After ACLs are disabled on an existing bucket, they are [no longer part of an access evaluation] (s3-object-ownership-disable-acls-existing-bucket). An account that received access [can't delegate permission cross-account to another AWS account] (s3-permission-delegation-no-second-cross-account-hop). A resource control policy sets the [maximum available permissions] on buckets in an organization (s3-change-rcp-for-s3-2024-11; chapter 04). A bucket policy is limited to [20 KB] (s3-bucket-policy-max-size). At most 110 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: across accounts, both sides must allow the read. The thing to watch is an explicit deny, which wins over every allow.
plan.stop_and_answer: The bucket policy in account A allows account B's role to call s3:GetObject on the bucket. The role's identity-based policy in account B allows only s3:ListBucket on that bucket. Can the role download an object? Answer: no; across accounts the request needs [permission from both the parent AWS account] and the bucket owner (s3-authorization-both-accounts-must-allow), and the role's own policy does not allow s3:GetObject.

sections.heading: Block Public Access overrides any policy or ACL that would make data public

plan.problem: A developer adds a bucket policy with "Principal": "*" so that a browser can play recordings. One policy edit must not be able to expose every customer's data.
trace: **The edit.** A wildcard principal [which effectively means "anyone"] (s3-best-practice-wildcard-principal-means-anyone); S3 [begins by assuming that the policy is public] and then checks it (s3-public-policy-definition).

**The four settings.** [BlockPublicAcls], [IgnorePublicAcls], [BlockPublicPolicy] and [RestrictPublicBuckets] (s3-block-public-access-four-settings-most-restrictive) are [turned on at the bucket level] by default (s3-block-public-access-default-on).
**The override.** The [settings override these policies and permissions] (s3-block-public-access-overrides-policies), so the public policy is refused or ignored.

**The levels.** Account and organization settings apply too, and S3 [applies the most restrictive combination] (s3-block-public-access-four-settings-most-restrictive); an organization policy can [override account-level settings] (s3-bpa-org-level-overrides-account).
plan.table: Where Block Public Access applies (columns: Level | Covers | Note): access point | that access point | each access point has its own settings; bucket | that bucket | on by default (s3-block-public-access-default-on); account | [applies to all buckets and access points] (s3-block-public-access-account-level-recommended) | all Regions; organization | the accounts in its scope | [all four settings are applied together] (s3-bpa-org-level-overrides-account); single object | not supported | not [on a per-object basis] (s3-block-public-access-not-per-object).
plan.why: Why a switch above the policies? Policies change often and many people write them; Block Public Access is [enforced regardless of how the resources are created] (s3-block-public-access-centralized-controls), and AWS recommends to [turn on all four settings] for the account (s3-block-public-access-account-level-recommended).
plan.exam_signal: "ensure that no bucket in the account can be made public" points to Block Public Access at the account level (or the organization level); IAM Access Analyzer for S3 only alerts you when a bucket allows access to [anyone on the internet] (s3-faq-access-analyzer-s3).
plan.body_extras: One sentence for websites: the S3 website endpoint serves only public content and does [do not support HTTPS or access points] (s3-website-endpoint-no-https); AWS points to [Amazon CloudFront to serve content from Amazon S3] (s3-war-avoid-public-buckets-use-cloudfront). Chapter 15 owns origin access control.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: keep Block Public Access on for the whole account. The thing to watch is that it only blocks access; it never edits the policy itself.
plan.stop_and_answer: Block Public Access is on at the account level. One bucket has all four bucket-level settings off and a bucket policy that allows public reads. Can anyone on the internet read its objects? Answer: no; S3 [applies the most restrictive combination] of the account and bucket settings (s3-block-public-access-four-settings-most-restrictive).

sections.heading: A presigned URL lends the permission of its signer until the URL expires

plan.problem: Customers must upload and play recordings in the browser, and the bucket must stay private. The browser has no AWS credentials.
trace: **Ask.** The browser asks the application for a link to one object.

**Sign.** The application signs a URL with its own credentials: the URL uses the credentials of the [principal who generated the URL] (s3-presigned-url-time-limited-creator-credentials). It sets an expiry: from the AWS CLI or an SDK, up to [7 days] (s3-presign-cli-sdk-expiration). Pending fr-0045: until it is filled, do not describe what the signature covers (method, key, expiry); say only that the application signs the URL.
**Use.** The browser sends GET or PUT straight to Amazon S3; a presigned URL allows [an upload without requiring another party] to have credentials (s3-presigned-url-upload-no-credentials-needed).

**Check.** S3 checks the expiry [at the time of the HTTP request] (s3-presigned-url-reusable-until-expiry) and allows only what the signer may do: the URL is [limited by the permissions of the user] who created it (s3-presigned-url-creator-needs-permission).
plan.table: When the URL stops working (columns: Signed with | Stops working at): long-term credentials, CLI or SDK | the expiry you set, at most [7 days] (s3-presign-cli-sdk-expiration); the S3 console | between [1 minute] and [12 hours] (s3-presign-console-expiration); temporary credentials of a role | the expiry or [the URL expires when the credential expires], [whichever occurs first] (s3-presigned-url-expires-with-temporary-credentials); an EC2 instance role | the end of the role credentials, [typically 6 hours] (s3-presign-ec2-role-duration).
plan.why: Why not make the bucket public for the browser? A presigned URL gives [time-limited access to objects in Amazon S3] without changing the bucket policy (s3-presigned-url-time-limited-creator-credentials), so the bucket stays private and each link opens one object.
plan.exam_signal: "users without AWS credentials must upload or download a private object for a limited time" points to a presigned URL (s3-presigned-url-time-limited-creator-credentials). For many files behind a CDN, chapter 15 teaches CloudFront signed URLs: an xref, no detail.
plan.body_extras: One or two sentences: a page on app.callvale.example that sends PUT to the bucket's domain is a cross-origin request; a CORS configuration lets web applications [interact with resources in a different domain] (s3-cors-purpose), and the request's Origin and method must match [AllowedOrigins] and [AllowedMethods] (s3-cors-rule-match-origin-method-headers). (The host name is a story name; keep the sentence free of other story facts.)
plan.try_it: Try it callout for s3-t02 after the table, ending with its task comment.
plan.spot_the_bug: Spot the bug (one of the two in the file): an application on an EC2 instance signs a download URL with its instance role, sets the expiry to 7 days and emails the URL to a customer; the next day the customer gets Access Denied. Reveal: the URL [expires when the role session ends] (s3-presigned-url-expires-with-temporary-credentials), which for an instance role is [typically 6 hours] (s3-presign-ec2-role-duration). Place it after the Exam trap and before Say it; about 70 words with its reveal.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: the app signs a short-lived link, and the browser talks to S3 directly. The thing to watch is that anyone who holds the link can use it until it expires.
plan.stop_and_answer: The application's role may call s3:GetObject only on keys under customer-17/. A developer uses that role to presign a URL for customer-42/call.wav. Does the URL work? Answer: no; a presigned URL is [limited by the permissions of the user] who created it (s3-presigned-url-creator-needs-permission).

sections.heading: Access points and Requester Pays control who reaches shared data and who pays

plan.problem: Five teams and two partners read one shared dataset. One bucket policy for all of them grows too large, and the bucket owner pays for every download.
trace: **Give each application its own door.** An access point is one of the [named network endpoints with dedicated access policies] (s3-access-point-definition); each has [its own access point policy] (s3-access-point-vpc-only).

**Lock a door to one VPC.** With a VPC network origin, S3 rejects any request that [doesn't originate from that VPC] (s3-access-point-network-origin-vpc), and [you can't change its network origin] later.

**Check both policies.** A request through an access point needs [both the access point and the underlying bucket] to allow it (s3-access-point-needs-bucket-permission-too); AWS recommends you [delegate access control for a bucket] to its access points.

**Let the reader pay.** With Requester Pays, [the requester instead of the bucket owner pays] for requests and downloads, and [the bucket owner always pays the cost] of storage (s3-requester-pays-who-pays). Each request carries [x-amz-request-payer] (s3-requester-pays-header-required), and [anonymous access to that bucket is not allowed] (s3-requester-pays-no-anonymous).
plan.table: Access options (columns: Option | Solves | Limit): access point | a policy for each application, beyond the bucket policy's [policy size limits of S3 bucket policies (20 KB) and IAM policies (5 KB)] (s3-access-points-scale-policy-space) | works only [to perform operations on objects] (s3-access-points-object-operations-only); VPC-only access point, or a bucket policy with [aws:SourceVpce] | traffic from one network only | a SourceVpce policy also [disables console access to the specified bucket] (s3-bucket-policy-source-vpce-condition); Requester Pays | the downloader pays requests and transfer | no anonymous access, and the website endpoint returns [403 Access Denied] (s3-website-requester-pays-403).
plan.why: Why access points instead of one big bucket policy? Each access point carries its own policy, which gives [significantly more space for policy statements] (s3-access-points-scale-policy-space) and one place to change one team's access.
plan.exam_signal: "share a large dataset; the requesters must pay for the data transfer" points to Requester Pays (s3-requester-pays-share-without-paying-access); "each application needs its own permissions on one shared bucket" points to S3 access points (s3-access-point-definition).
plan.body_extras: Optional half sentence, only if words remain: S3 Access Grants maps directory users and groups to data by prefix (s3-access-grants-identities). VPC endpoints themselves are chapter 10 and 11: an xref.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: give each application its own access point, and let downloaders pay with Requester Pays. The thing to watch is that the bucket policy must still allow the request.
plan.stop_and_answer: A partner who is signed in to its own AWS account downloads from a Requester Pays bucket but forgets the request-payer header. What happens, and who pays for that request? Answer: [Amazon S3 returns a 403 error and charges the bucket owner for the request] (s3-requester-pays-header-required; use the fact's display: 'Amazon S3 returns a 403 error and charges the bucket owner for the request').

sections.heading: Every new object is encrypted with SSE-S3 unless you choose another key

plan.problem: A customer's security questionnaire asks who holds the encryption keys and who can see each use of a key. The default answer may not be enough.
trace: **Default.** Every bucket has encryption configured, and new objects [are automatically encrypted at rest] with [SSE-S3] (s3-sse-s3-default-every-bucket); you can [no longer disable encryption] for new uploads (s3-default-encryption-cannot-disable).

**A KMS key.** With SSE-KMS, AWS KMS manages the key, [there are separate permissions] for its use, and the audit trail shows [who used your key to access which object] (s3-sse-kms-benefits-over-sse-s3). An S3 Bucket Key can cut KMS request costs by [up to 99 percent] (s3-bucket-key-kms-cost-up-to-99-percent).
**Your key on each request.** With SSE-C, S3 encrypts, but [S3 never stores the encryption key], and [You must use HTTPS] (s3-sse-c-key-never-stored-https-required).

**Encrypt before upload.** With client-side encryption, [you manage the encryption process, the encryption keys] (s3-client-side-encryption-you-manage-keys), and S3 [does not play a role in encrypting] (s3-client-side-encryption-not-exposed-to-aws).
plan.table: Who holds the key (columns: Option | Key held by | Choose it when): SSE-S3 | Amazon S3 | the default is enough; SSE-KMS | AWS KMS, under your key policy | [if you need more control over your keys] (s3-sse-kms-when-more-key-control) and an audit trail; DSSE-KMS | AWS KMS | you need [two layers of encryption to your data] (s3-dsse-kms-two-layers); SSE-C | you, sent with every request | keys stay outside AWS, but S3 does the encryption (s3-faq-sse-c-keys); client-side | you | data must be encrypted before it leaves you (s3-client-side-encryption-you-manage-keys).
plan.why: Why choose SSE-KMS over the default? The KMS key adds a second permission check and an audit record for each use (s3-sse-kms-benefits-over-sse-s3). Chapter 06 owns KMS keys and key policies: an xref.
plan.exam_signal: "the company must manage its own keys, and the keys must not be stored in AWS" points to SSE-C, or to client-side encryption when data must be encrypted before upload (s3-faq-sse-c-keys); "audit who used the key" points to SSE-KMS (s3-sse-kms-benefits-over-sse-s3).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: existing objects, SSE-C defaults and enforcement. A new default leaves objects already [in the bucket is not changed] (s3-default-encryption-change-not-retroactive); UpdateObjectEncryption changes the type [without any data movement] (s3-change-update-object-encryption-2026-01). Since [April 2026], new buckets have [SSE-C encryption disabled for all new write requests] (s3-change-sse-c-disabled-default-2026-04). A bucket policy can demand SSE-KMS with [s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption] (s3-bucket-policy-require-sse-kms-on-put) and HTTPS with [aws:SecureTransport] (s3-bucket-policy-secure-transport-https-only). The KMS key must be [in the same Region as the bucket] (s3-sse-kms-key-same-region-as-bucket). At most 110 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: S3 encrypts every new object for you. The thing to watch is who must hold the key: S3, KMS or your company.
plan.stop_and_answer: A partner's role in another account has s3:GetObject on the bucket. The objects are encrypted with SSE-KMS under the AWS managed key aws/s3. Can the partner read them? Answer: no; for cross-account access to SSE-KMS objects you need a customer managed key whose key policy allows the other account: [use a customer managed key] (s3-sse-kms-cross-account-needs-customer-managed-key).

sections.heading: Infrequent access classes add retrieval fees and a minimum storage duration
sections.diagram: s3-storage-class-ladder, after the table (its alt and caption count toward this subsection: keep the alt at about 40 words)

plan.problem: Recordings are read often in the first weeks and almost never after a few months. Paying the same storage price every month wastes money.
trace: **Upload.** Without a class in the request, [Amazon S3 assigns the S3 Standard storage class] (s3-storage-class-default-standard); the class is set [at the object level] (s3-storage-class-set-per-object).
**Read less often.** S3 Standard-IA keeps objects [available for millisecond access] but [charges a retrieval fee for these objects] (s3-ia-classes-millisecond-access-retrieval-fee).

**Leave early or store small.** An object deleted, overwritten or moved before [30 days] pays a [pro-rated charge for the remainder of the 30-day minimum] (s3-ia-min-duration-charge); an object below [128 KB] is billed as 128 KB (s3-ia-min-billable-size).

**Lose a zone.** S3 One Zone-IA keeps data in [1 Availability Zone] (s3-class-one-zone-ia-profile) and is [not resilient to the physical loss] of that zone (s3-one-zone-ia-az-loss); the other classes here keep data across [a minimum of three Availability Zones] (s3-durability-three-az-design).
plan.table: Classes you read directly (columns: Class | Availability Zones | Minimum duration | Retrieval fee): S3 Standard | three or more | none: N/A in (s3-min-duration-charge-table) | no; S3 Intelligent-Tiering | three or more | [no minimum storage duration] (s3-faq-it-no-min-duration) | [no retrieval charges] (s3-faq-it-no-retrieval-fees); S3 Standard-IA | three or more | [30 days] (s3-ia-min-duration-charge) | per GB (s3-faq-standard-ia-retrieval-charge); S3 One Zone-IA | [1 Availability Zone] (s3-class-one-zone-ia-profile) | [30 days] | per GB; S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval | three or more | [90 days] (s3-class-glacier-ir-profile) | per GB. 'three or more' cells link [a minimum of three Availability Zones] (s3-durability-three-az-design) once in the header row note or the first cell.
plan.why: Why fees and minimums? These classes charge less to store and more to read, so AWS says to choose by [access patterns and retention time] (s3-faq-storage-class-cost-structure) for the lowest total cost.
plan.exam_signal: "infrequently accessed data that can be re-created" points to S3 One Zone-IA; "the only copy" points to S3 Standard-IA, the class for the [primary or only copy of data] (s3-standard-ia-vs-one-zone-ia-use).
plan.body_extras: One sentence on durability and speed: every class is designed for eleven nines of durability, [99.999999999%] (s3-faq-durability-11-nines); S3 Express One Zone gives [single-digit millisecond data access] in one zone (s3-express-one-zone-single-digit-ms-single-az). Do not state a minimum storage duration for S3 Express One Zone (see notes_for_orchestrator).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: pay less to store, and more to read. The thing to watch is the minimum duration and the minimum object size.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team writes ten million small thumbnails, each well under the minimum billable size, to S3 Standard-IA and deletes each one after ten days. Which two charges make this costly? Answer: each object is billed as [128 KB] (s3-ia-min-billable-size), and each one pays for the full [30 days] (s3-ia-min-duration-charge).

sections.heading: Intelligent-Tiering moves an unread object to cheaper tiers with no retrieval fee

plan.problem: Nobody knows which old recordings customers will open again. A fixed rule could move a recording that is still popular into a class with retrieval fees.
trace: **Store it.** S3 watches each object's access for [a low monthly object monitoring and automation charge] (s3-intelligent-tiering-automatic-tiers).
**No reads.** After [30 consecutive days] without access the object moves to the Infrequent Access tier, and after [90 days] to the Archive Instant Access tier (s3-int-tiering-automatic-tiers).
**A read.** The object is [automatically moved back to the Frequent Access tier] (s3-int-tiering-move-back), with [no retrieval fees] (s3-int-tiering-no-retrieval-fees).

**Optional archive tiers.** If you turn them on, objects unread for a [minimum of 90 consecutive days] go to Archive Access and for a [minimum of 180 consecutive days] to Deep Archive Access, and must be restored before a read (s3-int-tiering-optional-archive-tiers).
plan.table: The tiers (columns: Tier | An object moves there after | First byte): Frequent Access | upload, or any read | milliseconds; Infrequent Access | [30 consecutive days] without access | milliseconds; Archive Instant Access | [90 days] without access | milliseconds (s3-int-tiering-archive-retrieval-times: the Archive Instant Access tier keeps millisecond access); Archive Access (optional) | at least 90 days | [3–5 hours] after a restore (s3-int-tiering-archive-retrieval-times); Deep Archive Access (optional) | at least 180 days | [within 12 hours] after a restore.
plan.why: Why no retrieval fee? The class charges per object for monitoring instead, which makes it [the default storage class for virtually any workload] whose access pattern is unknown (s3-intelligent-tiering-ideal-for-unknown-access).
plan.exam_signal: "unknown, changing or unpredictable access patterns" points to S3 Intelligent-Tiering (s3-intelligent-tiering-ideal-for-unknown-access).
plan.body_extras: One sentence, required: objects smaller than [128 KB] are not monitored and are [always stored in the Frequent Access tier] (s3-int-tiering-small-objects). Optional, only if words remain: Storage Class Analysis watches [the previous 30-90 days] and recommends a lifecycle transition (s3-storage-class-analysis-observation); S3 Storage Lens gives [organization-wide visibility into object storage usage] (s3-storage-lens-organization-view).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects for you, and reads cost no retrieval fee. The thing to watch is the monitoring charge on each object.
plan.stop_and_answer: An object in the Archive Instant Access tier is read once. Where is it the next day, and does the read add a retrieval fee? Answer: in the Frequent Access tier, because it is [automatically moved back to the Frequent Access tier] (s3-int-tiering-move-back), and there are [no retrieval fees] (s3-int-tiering-no-retrieval-fees).

sections.heading: Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive objects must be restored before anyone reads them

plan.problem: A customer asks for a recording from two years ago. In an archive class the object is listed in the bucket, but a plain GET does not return its data.
trace: **GET fails.** Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive data is [archived, and not available for real-time access] (s3-archive-classes-access-model); you first [retrieve data using the RestoreObject REST API] (s3-archive-restore-needed-flexible-deep). Glacier Instant Retrieval objects are [immediately available using GET].
**Restore.** You choose one of [Expedited, Standard and Bulk] and a number of days; [Standard is the default option] (s3-archive-retrieval-options-three).

**Wait.** From Flexible Retrieval: [1–5 minutes], [3–5 hours] or [5–12 hours] (s3-archive-retrieval-times-flexible). From Deep Archive: Expedited is [Not available], Standard [Within 12 hours], Bulk [Within 48 hours] (s3-archive-retrieval-times-deep). S3 can send an event when it is done: [`s3:ObjectRestore:Completed`] (s3-restore-completed-event).

**Read the copy.** S3 makes a temporary copy for the days you asked for, while [the object's storage class remains] archived (s3-archive-restore-temporary-copy); you pay for the archive and for the copy at the S3 Standard rate (s3-pricing-restore-pays-archive-plus-temporary-standard-copy).
plan.table: The three Glacier classes (columns: Class | First byte | Minimum duration | Cheapest retrieval): S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval | [Milliseconds] (s3-class-glacier-ir-compare-row) | [90 days] | a GET with a retrieval fee; S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval | [Minutes to 12 hours] (s3-class-glacier-flexible-compare-row) | [90 days] | Bulk, [free bulk retrievals] (s3-class-glacier-flexible-access-1-2-per-year); S3 Glacier Deep Archive | [9 to 48 hours] (s3-class-deep-archive-compare-row) | [180 days] | Bulk, within 48 hours (s3-retrieval-bulk-lowest-cost-48-hours-deep-archive).
plan.why: Why wait for a restore? The waiting buys the lowest storage price: Deep Archive is [the lowest cost storage in the cloud] (s3-class-deep-archive-lowest-cost-twelve-hours), and the three classes keep the [same durability and resiliency] as S3 Standard (s3-class-glacier-family-same-durability).
plan.exam_signal: "retrieval within 12 hours" with "lowest cost" points to S3 Glacier Deep Archive (s3-class-deep-archive-lowest-cost-twelve-hours); "some files are needed within minutes" points to Flexible Retrieval with Expedited (s3-retrieval-expedited-1-5-minutes-not-deep-archive); "rarely read, but needed immediately" points to Glacier Instant Retrieval (s3-class-glacier-ir-lowest-cost-milliseconds).
plan.body_extras: One sentence: the original Amazon Glacier vault service [is no longer accepting new customers], and AWS recommends the [Amazon Glacier storage classes in Amazon S3] (s3-glacier-change-vault-service-closed-2025-10); objects in these classes stay in S3: [your objects remain in Amazon S3] (s3-archive-objects-stay-in-s3).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: an archived object comes back as a temporary copy after a restore. The thing to watch is that Deep Archive has no Expedited option.
plan.stop_and_answer: Data in S3 Glacier Deep Archive must be readable eight hours after a request at the latest. Which retrieval option meets that? Answer: none; Standard finishes [Within 12 hours], Bulk [Within 48 hours], and Expedited is [Not available] (s3-archive-retrieval-times-deep). Store such data in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval instead.

sections.heading: A lifecycle rule moves objects one way to colder classes and then expires them

plan.problem: Recordings must be kept for years, but almost none are opened after a few months. Nobody can move millions of objects to cheaper storage by hand. (No story numbers in this paragraph: they belong in the Startup example callout.)
trace: **Write a rule.** A lifecycle configuration is [a set of rules that define actions] (s3-lifecycle-transition-and-expiration-actions); a rule can filter by [key prefix, object tags, or a combination] (s3-lifecycle-filter-prefix-tags-and) and applies to [both existing and new S3 objects] (s3-faq-lifecycle-existing-and-new).

**Transition.** Objects move down [a waterfall model for transitioning between storage classes] (s3-lifecycle-transition-waterfall); the move out of an archive class [can go only one way] (s3-lifecycle-no-transition-out-of-archive).

**Pay for the move.** Each transition is a request [charged per object] (s3-faq-lifecycle-transition-request-charge); by default the rule [prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned] (s3-lifecycle-small-object-default); leaving a class before its minimum is [charged for the remainder of that duration] (s3-lifecycle-early-transition-charge).
**Expire.** At the age you set, S3 deletes the object; you are [not charged for expiration] or for storage after it (s3-lifecycle-expired-object-not-charged).
plan.table: Allowed transitions (columns: From | Can move to | Cannot move to): S3 Standard | every other class of the waterfall (s3-lifecycle-transition-waterfall) | none; S3 Standard-IA | S3 One Zone-IA and the Glacier classes: [from S3 Standard-IA to S3 One Zone-IA] (s3-faq-standard-ia-tier-down) | S3 Standard; S3 One Zone-IA | Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive (s3-lifecycle-transition-waterfall) | the warmer classes; S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval | only [transitioned to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive] (s3-lifecycle-no-transition-out-of-archive) | every warmer class; S3 Glacier Deep Archive | none | every class: restore and copy instead, [make a temporary copy of the object first] (s3-lifecycle-no-transition-out-of-archive).
plan.why: Why one way? Lifecycle exists to lower cost as data ages; when rules overlap, S3 Lifecycle [optimizes for cost] (s3-lifecycle-conflict-cost-optimized).
plan.exam_signal: "move objects to a cheaper class after some days and delete them after some years" points to one S3 Lifecycle rule with a transition action and an expiration action (s3-faq-lifecycle-example-30-365).
plan.startup_example: Startup example callout (at most 60 words, story numbers only from uses_numbers lifecycle_infrequent_access_days, audio_retention_years, audio_opened_after_90_days_percent): Callvale's rule on callvale-audio moves recordings to S3 Standard-IA after 90 days and deletes them after 7 years; 2% of recordings are opened after 90 days. Transcripts stay in S3 Standard. No AWS rule in the callout; the reason that Standard-IA fits the only copy is linked in the sentence after it: [primary or only copy of data] (s3-standard-ia-primary-copy).
plan.spot_the_bug: Spot the bug (the second of the file): a rule on callvale-transcripts moves every transcript (30 KB on average) to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days; a month later the bill for that bucket has not fallen. Reveal: by default lifecycle [prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned] (s3-lifecycle-small-object-default), and with a size filter each transcript would be billed as [128 KB] in Standard-IA (s3-ia-min-billable-size); keep transcripts in S3 Standard. About 70 words with its reveal; story numbers only in the prompt (average_transcript_kb).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: when the rule runs and which rule wins. S3 counts days from creation and rounds to [the next day at midnight UTC] (s3-lifecycle-days-rounded-to-midnight-utc). Archive transitions can lag, but billing starts [from the date the lifecycle rule is satisfied] (s3-lifecycle-archive-transition-async-billing-at-rule-date). An object gets [only one S3 Lifecycle action per day] (s3-lifecycle-one-action-per-day), and [Permanent deletion takes precedence over transition] (s3-lifecycle-conflict-deletion-wins). You [can't use a bucket policy to prevent deletions] by a rule (s3-bucket-policy-cannot-stop-lifecycle). Since [2026-04-09], [S3 Lifecycle blocks expiration and transition actions] on objects whose replication failed (s3-change-lifecycle-pauses-failed-replication-2026-04). At most 110 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a lifecycle rule moves objects to colder classes as they age, then deletes them. The thing to watch is small objects and early moves, which cost more.
plan.stop_and_answer: One rule moves objects to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval on day 4 and to S3 Glacier Deep Archive on day 30. Can one rule do that? Answer: no; one rule cannot move an object out of a class before its minimum storage duration, so the Deep Archive step needs [at least 94 days] (s3-lifecycle-no-single-rule-before-minimum-duration).

sections.heading: Versioning turns a delete into a delete marker and keeps every version
sections.diagram: s3-versioning-states, after the trace (its alt and caption count toward this subsection: keep the alt at about 30 words)

plan.problem: An engineer runs a cleanup script against the wrong prefix and deletes thousands of recordings. In a bucket without versioning, deleted data [cannot be recovered by AWS] (s3-faq-delete-is-immediate).
trace: **Turn it on.** [S3 Versioning is disabled on buckets] by default (s3-versioning-off-by-default); once it is on, S3 gives [a unique version ID for each object], and objects stored before keep a [version ID of null] (s3-version-id-null-before-versioning).
**Overwrite.** A PUT to an existing key [creates another version of the object] (s3-upload-overwrite-creates-new-version).

**Delete without a version ID.** [Amazon S3 doesn't permanently delete the object]; a delete marker [becomes the current (or newest) version] (s3-delete-marker-soft-delete), and a plain GET returns [404 Not Found] (s3-versioning-get-delete-marker-404), while a GET that names an older version ID still returns it.

**Delete with a version ID.** [that object version is permanently deleted] and no marker is added (s3-versioning-delete-with-version-id-permanent). To get an object back after a plain delete, retrieve the earlier version: versions [can be retrieved or restored] (s3-versioning-preserves-on-overwrite-and-delete). Pending fr-0044: do not write that deleting the delete marker restores the object until the request is filled.
plan.table: One request, two kinds of bucket (columns: Request | Bucket without versioning | Versioning-enabled bucket): PUT to an existing key | replaces the object | adds a new version (s3-upload-overwrite-creates-new-version); DELETE without a version ID | deletes the object (s3-faq-delete-is-immediate) | adds a delete marker (s3-delete-marker-soft-delete); DELETE with a version ID | not used | deletes that version for good (s3-versioning-delete-with-version-id-permanent); GET after the delete | 404 | 404, but GET with an old version ID works (s3-versioning-get-delete-marker-404).
plan.why: Why keep every version? Durability [does not protect against accidental or malicious deletes] (s3-faq-durability-not-delete-protection); versioning lets you [recover from both unintended user actions] and application failures (s3-data-protection-mechanisms).
plan.exam_signal: "recover objects after an accidental delete or overwrite" points to S3 Versioning (s3-data-protection-mechanisms); "require MFA to delete a version permanently" points to MFA delete (s3-mfa-delete-protected-operations).
plan.body_extras: Two short sentences: normal rates [apply for every version of an object] (s3-versioning-every-version-billed), so pair versioning with a NoncurrentVersionExpiration rule, which can [permanently delete noncurrent versions of objects] (s3-lifecycle-noncurrent-version-expiration); a versioned bucket [can never return to an unversioned state] (s3-versioning-never-back-to-unversioned). MFA delete can be turned on [only the bucket owner (root account)], with the CLI or API (s3-mfa-delete-root-only-cli-api); AWS Backup [must activate S3 Versioning on your bucket] first (s3-aws-backup-requires-versioning; chapter 24).
plan.try_it: Try it callout for s3-t03 after the table, ending with its task comment.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: with versioning, a plain delete only hides the object behind a marker. The thing to watch is that every old version still costs storage.
plan.stop_and_answer: Versioning is suspended on a bucket that holds three versions of report.csv. What happens to the three versions? Answer: nothing; [existing objects in your bucket do not change] (s3-versioning-suspend-keeps-existing-versions); suspending only makes S3 [stop accruing new versions].

sections.heading: Object Lock compliance mode stops every user from deleting a version until its date

plan.problem: A bank requires call records that nobody can delete or change for years, an administrator included. Write the requirement as story text; if a sentence keeps an absolute word without a fact, end it with <!-- no-fact: requirement -->.
trace: **Prepare the bucket.** [Object Lock works only with versioned buckets], and you can [enable Object Lock for an existing S3 bucket] (s3-object-lock-enable-existing-bucket); afterwards you [cannot disable S3 Object Lock or S3 Versioning] (s3-faq-object-lock-cannot-disable).

**Lock a version.** A retention period or a legal hold [protects only the version that's specified] (s3-object-lock-requires-versioning); a bucket default retention sets the date for new versions by [adding the specified duration] to their creation time (s3-object-lock-bucket-default-retention).

**Choose the mode.** In governance mode, users cannot delete or change the lock [unless they have special permissions], namely [s3:BypassGovernanceRetention] (s3-object-lock-governance-mode). In compliance mode a version [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user], the root user included, and [its retention period can't be shortened] (s3-object-lock-compliance-mode).

**Try to delete.** A DELETE that names the version ID returns [Access Denied (403 Forbidden)]; a DELETE without it adds a delete marker, and [delete markers are not WORM-protected] (s3-object-lock-delete-behavior).
plan.table: Who can remove the protection (columns: Control | Ends | Who can remove or shorten it): governance retention | at its Retain Until Date | users with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention (s3-object-lock-governance-mode); compliance retention | at its Retain Until Date | no user; the only early path is to [delete the associated AWS account] (s3-object-lock-compliance-mode); legal hold | [it has no expiration date] (s3-object-lock-retention-vs-legal-hold) | any user with [s3:PutObjectLegalHold] (s3-object-lock-legal-hold-independent); versioning with MFA delete | not applicable | the bucket owner with [two forms of authentication] (s3-mfa-delete-protected-operations).
plan.why: Why two modes? AWS says to use governance mode when [some users with special permissions] may change retention or delete, and compliance mode when you [never want any user, including the root user] to delete during the retention period (s3-object-lock-mode-choice).
plan.exam_signal: "WORM" or "no user, including the root user, can delete or overwrite the records" points to Object Lock in compliance mode (s3-object-lock-compliance-mode); the model is [write-once-read-many (WORM) model] (s3-object-lock-worm-definition).
plan.body_extras: One sentence, choose one: a lifecycle expiration cannot delete a locked version: [locked version of an object cannot be deleted] (s3-object-lock-lifecycle-cannot-expire-locked); or a replication destination [must also have Object Lock enabled] (s3-object-lock-replication-destination). Object Lock variable retention (2026-09-08) is not examinable yet: leave it out.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: use compliance mode when nobody, not even the root user, may delete. The thing to watch is that you can never shorten it later.
plan.stop_and_answer: A version in compliance mode has a retain-until date in 2030. The security team wants to move the date to 2028. Can it? Answer: no; in compliance mode [its retention period can't be shortened] (s3-object-lock-compliance-mode); you can only extend it with a later date (s3-object-lock-retention-extend-only).

sections.heading: Replication copies new objects asynchronously and needs versioning on both buckets

plan.problem: A second copy of every recording must exist in another Region in case the first Region fails. A copy script misses files and costs engineering time.
trace: **Prepare.** Both buckets need versioning, and S3 [must have permissions to replicate objects] on your behalf (s3-replication-requires-versioning-both).

**A new object arrives.** S3 copies it with [automatic, asynchronous copying] (s3-faq-replication-async); live replication [replicates newly uploaded objects as they are written] (s3-batch-replication-for-existing-objects).
**Objects from before the rule.** S3 Batch Replication [allows you to replicate existing objects] (s3-batch-replication-for-existing-objects).

**A delete.** A DELETE that names a version ID is not copied: S3 [doesn't replicate the deletion in the destination buckets], which [protects data from malicious deletions] (s3-replication-version-deletes-not-replicated); delete markers are copied only with [delete marker replication enabled] (s3-replication-delete-markers-optional).
plan.table: Which copy (columns: Need | Use | Because): copies far away for compliance | Cross-Region Replication | to [store data at even greater distances] (s3-crr-for-compliance-distance-requirements); lower latency for users in another Region | Cross-Region Replication | to [minimize latency in accessing objects] (s3-crr-minimize-latency-copies-near-users); a copy in the same Region, in another account | Same-Region Replication | [separate AWS account in the same region] (s3-faq-srr-reasons); one endpoint for several Regions, with failover | a Multi-Region Access Point on replicated buckets | [single global endpoint] (s3-faq-crr-vs-mrap).
plan.why: Why asynchronous? The write to the source finishes first and the copy follows, so the source does not wait. When the copy time matters, S3 Replication Time Control is designed to copy [99.99% of objects within 15 minutes] (s3-replication-time-control-15-minutes).

Archived objects are not copied [until you restore them and copy them] (s3-replication-archived-objects-not-replicated); replicas made by another rule are not copied again (s3-replication-replicas-not-rereplicated); lifecycle and other bucket settings are [not applied to the destination bucket] (s3-replication-bucket-config-not-replicated). traps.belief: Eleven nines of durability mean that data in S3 needs no versioning, replication or backup.
traps.truth: Durability protects against hardware loss, not against accidental or malicious deletes; a deleted object cannot be recovered by AWS. Versioning, Object Lock, replication or AWS Backup protect against deletes.

traps.belief: S3 One Zone-IA is fine for the only copy of important data, because it has the same eleven nines of durability.
traps.truth: S3 One Zone-IA keeps data in one Availability Zone and is not resilient to the loss of that zone; use it for data you can re-create, and S3 Standard-IA for the only copy.

traps.belief: Any S3 Glacier object can be read in minutes, either with a normal GET or with an Expedited retrieval.
traps.truth: Objects in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive must be restored to a temporary copy first; Expedited works only for Flexible Retrieval, and Deep Archive takes up to 12 hours (Standard) or 48 hours (Bulk). Only S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval answers a GET at once.

traps.belief: With versioning on, nobody can delete data from the bucket for good.
traps.truth: A DELETE that names a version ID deletes that version permanently, so anyone with that permission can still destroy data; MFA delete adds a second factor, and only Object Lock in compliance mode stops every user.

traps.belief: Turning on replication also copies the objects that are already in the bucket.
traps.truth: Live replication copies objects written after the rule exists; existing objects need S3 Batch Replication.

traps.belief: One PUT request can upload an object of any size up to the S3 maximum, and that maximum is 5 TB.
traps.truth: A single PUT uploads at most 5 GB; a larger object needs multipart upload, and since December 2025 the maximum object size is 50 TB.

traps.belief: To share objects with another AWS account, you add the account to the object ACL.
traps.truth: New buckets have ACLs disabled (Bucket owner enforced), requests that set ACLs fail, and AWS recommends keeping ACLs disabled; grant access with a bucket policy, plus an identity-based policy in the other account.

traps.belief: A bucket policy that allows public reads makes the objects public, even when Block Public Access is on.
traps.truth: Block Public Access settings override policies and ACLs, and S3 applies the most restrictive combination of the access point, bucket, account and organization settings.

traps.belief: A presigned URL carries its own permission: any signer can open any object with it, and it works for the full expiry time that was set.
traps.truth: A presigned URL is limited by the permissions of the principal who signed it, and a URL signed with temporary credentials stops working when those credentials expire, whichever comes first.

traps.belief: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key meets a requirement that the encryption keys stay with the company and are never stored in AWS.
traps.truth: With SSE-KMS the key lives in AWS KMS; when the keys must stay with the company, use SSE-C (S3 encrypts but never stores the key) or client-side encryption (you encrypt before upload).

traps.belief: S3 Standard-IA is always cheaper than S3 Standard for data that is read rarely.
traps.truth: Standard-IA bills each object as at least 128 KB, charges at least 30 days of storage, and adds a per-GB retrieval fee; small or short-lived objects can cost more there, and an unknown access pattern fits S3 Intelligent-Tiering.

traps.belief: A lifecycle rule can move archived objects back to S3 Standard when customers start to read them again.
traps.truth: Lifecycle transitions go one way down the waterfall; to bring an archived object back, restore a temporary copy and copy it with the new storage class.

traps.belief: Object Lock in governance mode stops every user, administrators included, from deleting a locked version.
traps.truth: In governance mode a user with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention who sends the bypass header can delete or change the lock; only compliance mode stops every user, the root user included.

traps.belief: An administrator or the root user can remove Object Lock compliance mode early when a legal or business need arises.
traps.truth: In compliance mode no user, the root user included, can delete a protected version or shorten its retention; when a privileged team must be able to remove the protection, use governance mode with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by questions-21-2 on 2026-10-12 for rule Q205)

traps.belief: With SSE-C, AWS never sees the unencrypted data, because the customer provides the key.
traps.truth: With SSE-C, Amazon S3 receives the data and performs the encryption and decryption with the key that the request carries; only client-side encryption keeps unencrypted data away from AWS.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by questions-21-2 on 2026-10-12 for rule Q205)

traps.belief: An S3 event notification can send events directly to any Amazon SQS queue, FIFO queues included.
traps.truth: SQS FIFO queues and SNS FIFO topics are not supported as S3 event notification destinations; send the events to Amazon EventBridge and route them with a rule.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by questions-21-2 on 2026-10-12 for rule Q205)

traps.belief: A bucket can be limited to one VPC with a security group, as an instance can.
traps.truth: S3 access is controlled by policies and settings (IAM policies, bucket policies, access point policies, VPC endpoint policies, Block Public Access); a VPC-only access point or an aws:SourceVpce condition limits access to a VPC.

options: a public bucket with long random object names

reasons_with_facts: Option 1 fails the privacy requirement: a public policy names a wildcard principal [which effectively means "anyone"] (s3-best-practice-wildcard-principal-means-anyone); AWS asks that [your S3 bucket is not public] unless anyone on the internet must read it (s3-best-practice-bucket-not-public), and Block Public Access is [turned on at the bucket level] by default (s3-block-public-access-default-on). A long name is not an access control: anyone with the link can still download (story, no fact needed).

Option 2 keeps the bucket private but makes the one instance carry every upload and every playback; a presigned URL allows [an upload without requiring another party] to have AWS credentials (s3-presigned-url-upload-no-credentials-needed), so the instance need not carry the bytes.

Option 3 gives [time-limited access to objects in Amazon S3] without changing the bucket policy (s3-presigned-url-time-limited-creator-credentials), and each link can do only what the application's role may do: [limited by the permissions of the user] (s3-presigned-url-creator-needs-permission). The application must create one URL for each transfer.

question_slots.note: Changed phrase: 'The images are the only copy and must remain available if an Availability Zone is lost.' Key: (A) S3 Standard-IA (s3-standard-ia-vs-one-zone-ia-use, s3-standard-ia-primary-copy). Option B carries trap s3-trap-one-zone-for-only-copy. The twin line quotes the changed phrase of q01.

question_slots.twin: first of strict twin pair C (twin q10)
question_slots.note: A company stores contracts in S3 and manages its own encryption keys in its data center. Changed phrase: 'Amazon S3 must perform the encryption and decryption, but the encryption keys must never be stored in AWS.' Key: (B) SSE-C (s3-faq-sse-c-keys, s3-sse-c-key-never-stored-https-required). Options identical in q10: (A) SSE-KMS with a customer managed key (trap s3-trap-kms-keys-on-premises); (B) SSE-C, sending the key with each request over HTTPS; (C) client-side encryption with the company's keys before upload; (D) SSE-S3 (misconception: S3 holds the key). Do not let the stem need AWS services to read the objects.

Application logs are read often for 30 days, rarely until day 90, then kept until year 7 for audits; an auditor can wait up to 12 hours; logs must be deleted after 7 years. Key: one lifecycle rule: S3 Standard-IA at day 30, S3 Glacier Deep Archive at day 90, expire at 7 years (s3-lifecycle-transition-waterfall, s3-faq-lifecycle-example-30-365, s3-class-deep-archive-lowest-cost-twelve-hours). Distractors: Deep Archive at day 30 and back to S3 Standard on each audit (trap s3-trap-lifecycle-back-to-standard); S3 One Zone-IA for the audit years (trap s3-trap-one-zone-for-only-copy); S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval with Expedited for every audit read (violates-qualifier: costs more than needed when 12 hours is acceptable; trap how-the-exam-asks-trap-cheapest-wins is not right here, use a misconception). Logs are larger than 128 KB.

Changed phrase: 'Most users must not be able to delete a record, but the security team must be able to remove the protection when a legal request requires it.' Key: (B) Object Lock in governance mode, with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention for the security team (s3-object-lock-governance-mode, s3-object-lock-mode-choice). Same four options as q04; option C carries trap s3-trap-versioning-stops-deletes.

A company enables Cross-Region Replication on a versioned bucket that already holds 2 years of objects; new objects appear in the destination, older ones do not. LEAST operational overhead to copy the older objects too. Key: S3 Batch Replication (s3-batch-replication-for-existing-objects). Distractors: wait, because replication copies existing objects in the background (trap s3-trap-replication-copies-existing); enable versioning on the destination bucket (misconception: it is already required for the rule to work, s3-replication-requires-versioning-both); a script that copies every object with the AWS CLI (violates-qualifier: overhead).

Changed phrase: 'The data must be encrypted before it leaves the company's data center, and AWS must never see the unencrypted data.' Key: (C) client-side encryption (s3-client-side-encryption-you-manage-keys, s3-client-side-encryption-not-exposed-to-aws). Same four options as q06; option A carries trap s3-trap-kms-keys-on-premises, option B (SSE-C) is the sibling-confusion distractor: S3 receives the plaintext.

A company has 200 buckets in one account; developers sometimes add bucket policies that allow public reads. The company must ensure that no bucket in the account can be made public, now or later. Key: turn on all four Block Public Access settings at the account level (s3-block-public-access-account-level-recommended, s3-block-public-access-overrides-policies). Distractors: IAM Access Analyzer for S3 alerts (trap how-the-exam-asks-trap-detect-meets-ensure); an AWS Config rule that reports public buckets (trap detection-trap-config-rule-prevents); a reviewer who checks every bucket policy each week (trap s3-trap-bucket-policy-beats-bpa is not this one; use a misconception; violates-qualifier: overhead). Optional: the stem can say 'one account' so that the organization-level setting is not needed.

An application in account B runs with an IAM role and must read objects from a bucket in account A, with least privilege; objects use SSE-S3. Select TWO. Keys: a bucket policy in account A that allows the role's ARN s3:GetObject on the bucket's objects; an identity-based policy on the role in account B that allows s3:GetObject on that bucket (s3-authorization-both-accounts-must-allow). Distractors: add account B to each object ACL (trap s3-trap-acl-cross-account); a bucket policy with Principal '*' and a condition on account B's name in the user agent (trap iam-trap-wildcard-principal-means-account); create an IAM user in account A and store its access key in the application (trap iam-trap-keys-on-instance).

A research team must store single files of 30 TB each in Amazon S3 and upload them from its data center. Key: upload each file with multipart upload (s3-mpu-object-size-range, s3-object-max-size). Distractors: one PUT request per file with a long timeout (trap s3-trap-single-put-any-size); split each file into 5 TB objects because S3 cannot store larger objects (trap s3-trap-single-put-any-size: the old maximum; difficulty 1 allows the same trap twice only if the beliefs differ, so tag this one with a misconception instead); upload in the S3 console (misconception: the console limit is [160 GB], s3-console-upload-max). Keep one impossible-feature at most.

Old call recordings must be kept for 10 years; auditors ask for a few files twice a year; a wait of 48 hours is acceptable. MOST cost-effective. Key: S3 Glacier Deep Archive and a Bulk restore when needed (s3-retrieval-bulk-lowest-cost-48-hours-deep-archive, s3-class-deep-archive-lowest-cost-twelve-hours). Distractors: Deep Archive with Expedited retrievals (trap s3-trap-glacier-read-directly: not available); S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (violates-qualifier: works, higher storage cost; trap how-the-exam-asks-trap-works-means-correct); S3 Standard-IA with a lifecycle rule (trap s3-trap-ia-always-cheaper).

A research institute shares a large genomics dataset with partner organizations that have their own AWS accounts; the institute wants to avoid paying for the partners' downloads. Key: enable Requester Pays on the bucket (s3-requester-pays-who-pays, s3-requester-pays-share-without-paying-access). Distractors: presigned URLs for each partner (misconception: the owner still pays for the downloads, s3-faq-cross-account-access-billing); a CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket (misconception: the owner pays); replicate the dataset into each partner's bucket (misconception: the source account pays for data transfer, s3-faq-replication-cross-account-who-pays). Tag at least two distractors with how-the-exam-asks-trap-works-means-correct where the option works but fails the cost requirement.

Medical images are kept for years and read about once a quarter; when a doctor opens one, it must load in milliseconds. MOST cost-effective. Key: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (s3-faq-instant-retrieval-once-a-quarter, s3-class-glacier-ir-lowest-cost-milliseconds). Distractors: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval with Expedited (trap s3-trap-glacier-read-directly); S3 Standard-IA (violates-qualifier: higher storage cost, s3-class-glacier-ir-vs-standard-ia); S3 Intelligent-Tiering with the Deep Archive Access tier turned on (misconception: that tier needs a restore, s3-int-tiering-optional-archive-tiers). Images larger than 128 KB.

A company relies on S3 durability. An employee deleted important objects by mistake and they could not be recovered. The company must be able to recover from accidental deletes and overwrites in the future, with the LEAST operational overhead. Key: enable S3 Versioning on the bucket (s3-data-protection-mechanisms, s3-delete-marker-soft-delete), optionally with a NoncurrentVersionExpiration rule. Wrong path for step 3: 'nothing to do, S3 already keeps several copies'; step 5 starts 'My first idea breaks because' durability does not protect against deletes (s3-faq-durability-not-delete-protection). Distractors: no change, durability is enough (trap s3-trap-durability-is-backup); a nightly script that copies the bucket to another bucket (violates-qualifier: overhead; also copies the deletes); S3 One Zone-IA copy (trap s3-trap-one-zone-for-only-copy).

A versioned bucket's storage grows every month, although the number of current objects is stable; Storage Lens shows many incomplete multipart uploads. Select TWO. Keys: a lifecycle rule with NoncurrentVersionExpiration (s3-lifecycle-noncurrent-version-expiration); a lifecycle rule with AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload (s3-lifecycle-abort-incomplete-multipart). Distractors: an Expiration action for current versions to remove incomplete uploads (misconception: [don't remove incomplete multipart uploads], s3-lifecycle-expiration-keeps-incomplete-mpu); suspend versioning to delete the old versions (misconception: [existing objects in your bucket do not change], s3-versioning-suspend-keeps-existing-versions; tag trap s3-trap-versioning-stops-deletes only if the option text states that belief, else misconception); move noncurrent versions to S3 One Zone-IA (trap s3-trap-one-zone-for-only-copy if the stem says they are the only copy).

Users on several continents upload files of several gigabytes to one bucket in us-east-1; uploads from far away are slow. LEAST operational overhead. Key: S3 Transfer Acceleration (s3-transfer-acceleration-when-to-use, s3-transfer-acceleration-how-it-works). Distractors: a bucket in each Region with Cross-Region Replication to us-east-1 (works, more overhead: trap how-the-exam-asks-trap-works-means-correct); AWS Direct Connect from each user site (misconception: private networking for distributed users, s3-faq-ta-vs-direct-connect); larger single PUT requests (trap s3-trap-single-put-any-size). Files are larger than 1 GB, so CloudFront PUT/POST is not the better answer (s3-transfer-acceleration-vs-cloudfront-small-objects).

Each upload to a bucket must start processing; the processing team requires an Amazon SQS FIFO queue. LEAST development effort. Key: send S3 events to Amazon EventBridge and route them with a rule to the FIFO queue (s3-event-notifications-no-fifo-destinations, s3-eventbridge-all-events-more-targets). Distractors: an S3 event notification directly to the FIFO queue (impossible-feature, why links s3-event-notifications-no-fifo-destinations); a Lambda function that polls the bucket every minute (misconception: more code); S3 Replication to a second bucket that triggers the queue (misconception). The stem must not need ordering guarantees from S3 itself (s3-event-notifications-no-order-duplicates).

A bucket holds 300 million JSON results of about 20 KB each, read rarely after the first week. A new lifecycle rule to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days did not lower the bill. Key: keep the small objects in S3 Standard (or aggregate them first): by default lifecycle does not transition objects under 128 KB, and Standard-IA bills each object as 128 KB (s3-lifecycle-small-object-default, s3-ia-min-billable-size). Distractors: add an object size filter so that the small objects transition (trap s3-trap-ia-always-cheaper); move them to S3 Intelligent-Tiering (misconception: objects under 128 KB are not auto-tiered, s3-int-tiering-small-objects); transition to S3 Glacier Deep Archive (misconception: per-object metadata overhead, s3-lifecycle-glacier-overhead-40-kb-per-object).

Several application teams share one bucket; the analytics team's access must work only from its VPC and must not change the access of the other teams, with the LEAST effect on the bucket policy. Key: an access point for the analytics team with a VPC network origin and its own access point policy, and the bucket policy delegating to access points (s3-access-point-network-origin-vpc, s3-access-point-needs-bucket-permission-too). Distractors: a bucket policy with aws:SourceVpce for the whole bucket (misconception: it would block the other teams and the console, s3-bucket-policy-source-vpce-condition); a security group attached to the bucket (impossible-feature; give its why a fact: access control mechanisms of S3 are listed in s3-faq-access-control-mechanisms); a NAT gateway for the VPC (trap vpc-trap-s3-needs-nat).

tasks.title: Read the settings that keep a new bucket private
tasks.kills: "A new bucket is public and unencrypted until you lock it down."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, read-only, 3 minutes, $0: read the account-level Block Public Access settings (aws s3control get-public-access-block with the account ID from aws sts get-caller-identity); state the expected output (four settings true), and the error the call returns when the account has no account-level configuration, in which case the bucket-level defaults still apply (s3-block-public-access-default-on). List buckets; for one bucket the reader owns, read get-public-access-block and get-bucket-encryption (expected: SSE-S3, shown as AES256: s3-sse-s3-default-every-bucket, s3-bucket-policy-require-sse-kms-on-put for the AES256 name). If the reader owns no bucket, read only the account setting and stop. Creates nothing. Commands from official CLI pages in the corpus (tasks check-cli --reference).

tasks.title: Share a private object with a presigned URL that expires
tasks.kills: "A browser can download from a private bucket only if the bucket is made public."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, one bucket and one small text object, cost about $0 (s3-faq-no-minimum-charge for the cost line): create a bucket saa-s3-t02-<random suffix> (bucket names are global: s3-bucket-name-global-namespace-default) and tag it book=saa and task=s3-t02; upload a small text file. Read the plain object URL with curl: expect 403 AccessDenied, because the bucket is private (s3-private-by-default). Presign a GET URL with aws s3 presign and a short --expires-in (for example 120 seconds); curl it: the file comes back. Break it: predict, wait past the expiry, curl again: expect 403 with a 'Request has expired' message, because S3 checks the expiry [at the time of the HTTP request] (s3-presigned-url-reusable-until-expiry). Note that CloudShell uses temporary credentials, so the URL also stops when they expire (s3-presigned-url-expires-with-temporary-credentials). Fix: presign again. Cleanup: delete the object, delete the bucket. Verify: aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources with the tag filter task=s3-t02 returns nothing (T108). Label 'checked against docs, not run in a real account'.

tasks.title: Delete a versioned object and get it back
tasks.kills: "In a versioned bucket a delete removes the object, and a delete can never destroy data for good."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, one bucket and two tiny object versions, cost about $0: create saa-s3-t03-<random suffix>, tag book=saa and task=s3-t03; turn on versioning (put-bucket-versioning Enabled); upload note.txt twice with different text; list-object-versions shows two version IDs. Break it: predict, then delete note.txt without a version ID; list-object-versions shows a delete marker as the latest version (s3-delete-marker-soft-delete); head-object returns 404 (s3-versioning-get-delete-marker-404). Fix: get-object with the newest real version ID returns the data (s3-versioning-get-delete-marker-404); copy that version back as the current object (copy-object with versionId in the source), so the plan does not depend on fr-0044; if fr-0044 is filled, also show deleting the marker. Cleanup: delete every version and the marker by version ID, which deletes them permanently (s3-versioning-delete-with-version-id-permanent: the step that kills the second half of the misconception), then delete the bucket. Verify by the tag task=s3-t03 (T108).

speak.prompt: How can a customer upload directly to our bucket if the bucket is private?
speak.note: Ana uses no AWS terms: explain 'presigned URL' as 'a signed, short-lived link' the first time. Short answer: our application gives the browser a signed link for one file, and the browser sends the file straight to the bucket; the bucket stays private. How it works: the application signs the link with its own permissions and sets a short expiry; S3 checks the signature and the time. Watch: anyone who holds the link can use it until it expires, so keep the expiry short. In your case: 'How long does a customer need to finish an upload on a slow connection?' Must not say: 'the link works only once'; 'the customer needs an AWS account'; 'the bucket must be public for a moment'.

speak.persona: a startup founder in office hours
speak.prompt: Should I put my old files in S3 Standard-IA or in Intelligent-Tiering?
speak.note: First sentence may start 'Both'. Short answer: if you know the files are read about once a month or less, Standard-IA; if you do not know, Intelligent-Tiering. How it works: Standard-IA charges a retrieval fee and a minimum of 30 days; Intelligent-Tiering moves each object by its own access with no retrieval fee, for a small monitoring charge per object. Watch: very small files stay in the frequent tier in Intelligent-Tiering and are billed as larger files in Standard-IA (spoken form of the facts; numbers allowed only as the facts' spoken forms). In your case: 'Do you know which files your users open again, and how big are they?' Must not say: 'Intelligent-Tiering has retrieval fees'; 'Standard-IA is always cheaper for old files'.

speak.prompt: Object Lock governance mode or compliance mode: which one should we turn on for our records?
speak.note: First sentence may start 'Both'. Short answer: both stop normal users from deleting a locked version; compliance mode also stops administrators and the root user, and its date cannot be moved earlier. How it works: governance mode lets a user with a special permission bypass the lock. Watch: compliance mode cannot be undone, and Object Lock cannot be turned off on the bucket afterwards; test with governance mode first. In your case: 'Does your regulator require that nobody, not even your administrators, can delete a record early?' Must not say: 'governance mode stops everyone'; 'you can shorten a compliance retention with root access'.

speak.prompt: S3 already has eleven nines of durability. Why should we pay for versioning or backups?
speak.note: Short answer: durability protects you from lost disks, not from your own delete commands; versioning protects you from those. How it works: with versioning, a delete adds a marker and the old version stays; a lifecycle rule removes old versions after some days so the bill stays small. Watch: every old version is billed until it expires. In your case: 'If someone deleted a customer's recordings by mistake this morning, how would you get them back?' Must not say: 'AWS can restore a deleted object'; 'versioning stops all deletes'.
